lead: An Android screen is not one drawing but a tree of small parts. Each part is a View: a button, a line of text, an image. A special View called a ViewGroup holds other views and decides where they sit. The activity window has one root ViewGroup, and every widget on the screen hangs below it. This tree is why Android screens are easy to change: move one branch, and only that part changes. You write the tree in XML, the activity inflates it in onCreate, and the user sees the result.
prereq: You need: Unit 2, activities and the activity life cycle, because a layout is inflated inside onCreate.

sections.h3: Views, view groups and the screen tree

blocks.text: A View occupies a rectangle on the screen and draws itself. It also receives touch events. A ViewGroup is a View with children. The group measures each child, places it, and passes touches down. Because a ViewGroup is itself a View, groups can nest: a vertical LinearLayout can hold a horizontal LinearLayout, which holds three buttons. The activity window holds exactly one root ViewGroup. Everything else is a descendant. This parent-child relation is the screen tree.

Every view shares a set of XML attributes. The id gives the view a name you can find from Java: android:id='@+id/saveButton'. The + means create the id if it does not exist. Width and height take match_parent (fill the parent), wrap_content (just big enough for the content) or a fixed size in dp. Padding is space inside the view, between its border and its content. Margin is space outside, between this view and its neighbours. Background sets a colour or drawable. Visibility is visible, invisible (hidden but still takes space) or gone (hidden and takes no space). enabled='false' blocks clicks and often greys the view.

A layout is a ViewGroup with a placement rule. LinearLayout puts children in one line, set by android:orientation to horizontal or vertical. Extra space can be shared by android:layout_weight. If three buttons in a horizontal row have weights 1, 2 and 3, the free space is cut into 1+2+3=6 parts and shared in that ratio. For weights to work cleanly, set the child's layout_width to 0dp in a horizontal layout (or layout_height to 0dp in a vertical one). Then the child does not first ask for its content width; the weight decides the whole width. weightSum sets the total by hand when you want a weight to mean a fraction of a fixed total.

Other layouts answer other questions. RelativeLayout places a child relative to the parent or to a sibling: layout_alignParentRight='true', layout_below='@id/title', layout_toRightOf='@id/icon'. FrameLayout stacks children in order; the last child is drawn on top, so it suits a badge over an image. TableLayout makes rows, and stretchColumns names columns that share leftover width. ConstraintLayout ties each child to the parent or to siblings with constraints, such as start to parent start and end to parent end; a child with both horizontal constraints and width 0dp spreads between them. GridLayout uses row and column indexes. Some syllabi call this 'designing by declaration' and call layouts 'screen containers'.

Sizes on Android are not pixels. A dp is a density-independent pixel: 1 dp is 1 pixel on a 160 dpi baseline screen and grows on denser screens so the physical size stays about the same. The conversion is:

blocks.where: px is device pixels; dp is the density-independent size; dpi is the screen density in dots per inch.

blocks.text: Text uses sp, a scale-independent pixel. It is like dp but also follows the user's font-size setting. Use dp for margins, padding and view sizes; use sp for text. A button height of 48 dp and a text size of 16 sp are typical Android choices.

Do not hard-code repeated strings, sizes and colours in the layout. Put them in res/values/strings.xml, dimens.xml and colors.xml, then refer to them as @string/app_name, @dimen/margin_small and @color/brand_blue. This keeps one change in one place and helps translation. The layout itself lives in res/layout/. When the activity calls setContentView(R.layout.main), Android inflates the XML into the view tree. State kept across rotation is a separate problem; see 3.2.

figure.caption: The row is 360 dp wide. Weight 1, 2 and 3 give buttons of 60, 120 and 180 dp; the widths fill the row exactly.

spec.aria: A horizontal LinearLayout of width 360 dp with three weighted buttons whose widths work out to 60, 120 and 180 dp.

examples.question: A horizontal LinearLayout is match_parent wide on a screen 360 dp wide. It holds three buttons, each with layout_width = 0dp and layout_weight = 1, 2 and 3. Find each button's width in dp, and in pixels on a 480 dpi screen. Show the check that the widths add to the row width.
steps: Button A = 1 × 60 = 60 dp; Button B = 2 × 60 = 120 dp; Button C = 3 × 60 = 180 dp.
Check: 60 + 120 + 180 = 360 dp, which is the full row.
examples.answer: Button A is 60 dp (180 px), B is 120 dp (360 px), C is 180 dp (540 px), and the three widths add to 360 dp.
examples.check:
total_width = 360
weights = [1, 2, 3]
dpi = 480
total_weight = sum(weights)
unit = total_width / total_weight
widths_dp = [w * unit for w in weights]
density = dpi / 160
widths_px = [w * density for w in widths_dp]
for value in widths_dp + widths_px:
    print(int(value))

traps: gravity centres a layout's own children, while layout_gravity places that view inside its parent. Swapping them is the most common layout bug.
Weights share space cleanly only when the child's width is 0dp in a horizontal layout. With match_parent the child already asks for the whole row, so the arithmetic gives surprising widths.
Margin is outside a view; padding is inside. A margin pushes neighbours away; padding moves the content within the border.
Use dp for sizes and sp for text. Text set in dp ignores the user's font-size setting, and a fixed px value breaks across screens.
invisible keeps the view's space; gone removes the space as well. Use gone when a hidden row should not leave a gap.

quiz.a: A ViewGroup is a View that holds and positions child views; every layout is a ViewGroup.

quiz.q: Why does a horizontal LinearLayout with weighted children usually set each child to 0dp width?
quiz.a: With 0dp the weight decides the whole width. With match_parent the child first asks for all the parent's width, so leftover space and the final widths become misleading.

quiz.q: A vertical LinearLayout is match_parent high on a 480 dp screen. Two children have layout_height=0dp and weights 1 and 3. Find their heights.
quiz.a: Weights add to 4; one unit is 480 ÷ 4 = 120 dp; heights are 120 dp and 360 dp.

quiz.q: A button sits in a LinearLayout. The developer wants the button's text centred but writes android:layout_gravity='center'. What happens, and what should be used?
quiz.a: layout_gravity centres the button inside the parent, not its text. Use android:gravity='center' on the button to centre the text.

quiz.q: What do match_parent and wrap_content mean for layout_width?
quiz.a: match_parent makes the view fill its parent's width; wrap_content makes it just wide enough for its content.

quiz.q: A horizontal LinearLayout is 320 dp wide. Three children have width 0dp and weights 2, 3 and 5. Find their widths in dp and pixels on a 320 dpi screen.
quiz.a: Weights total 10; one unit is 320 ÷ 10 = 32 dp; widths are 64, 96 and 160 dp. Density is 320 ÷ 160 = 2, so pixels are 128, 192 and 320 px.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real Android teams often build screens in ConstraintLayout with the visual editor, then add MotionLayout when a view must animate between states. Newer curricula also introduce Jetpack Compose, where layouts are functions rather than XML, but the same ideas of parent, child, size and weight remain. Accessibility checks ask whether every view has a label and whether touch targets are large enough. Search next for Android ConstraintLayout barriers and Jetpack Compose layout modifiers.
